lead: This unit sets out the parts of a circuit and the laws that tie them together. You learn how resistors, inductors and capacitors relate voltage to current, how independent and dependent sources drive them, and how Ohm's and Kirchhoff's laws turn any circuit into equations. After it you can count the equations a circuit needs, reduce series, parallel, star and delta networks, transform sources, and read a circuit as a graph.
about: The unit builds the language of circuit analysis in eight steps. The element laws of R, L and C come first, then the sources that drive them, then Ohm's law and Kirchhoff's two laws. Network terminology names the parts so that equations can be counted. Series-parallel reduction with voltage and current division, star-delta transformation and source transformation then shrink a network before it is solved, and network topology turns the circuit into a graph whose tree picks a complete set of independent equations. One bridge circuit runs through the terminology, star-delta and topology chapters, so you can check one method against another.

chapters.idea: Each passive element fixes a relation between voltage and current, and that relation decides how the element stores or dissipates energy.
chapters.depth: Define resistance R (ohm, Ω), inductance L (henry, H), capacitance C (farad, F). Give v = iR, v = L di/dt, i = C dv/dt. State that R dissipates p = vi = i²R, L stores ½Li², C stores ½Cv². Mark linear, passive, bilateral. Some syllabi call the V-I plot the volt-ampere characteristic. Mention ideal versus real: a real inductor has winding resistance.

figure.title: Passive element laws
figure.aria: Three passive element boxes feed a power box, which feeds an energy box.

chapters.example: A 12 Ω resistor carries 2 A. A 0.5 H inductor has di/dt = 40 A/s. A 100 μF capacitor has dv/dt = 200 V/s and 10 V across it. Find v_R, v_L, i_C, and the stored energies. Answers: v_R = 12 × 2 = 24 V; v_L = 0.5 × 40 = 20 V; i_C = 100×10⁻⁶ × 200 = 0.02 A = 20 mA; energy in L = ½ × 0.5 × 2² = 1 J; energy in C = ½ × 100×10⁻⁶ × 10² = 5 mJ.
chapters.trap: Using v = iR for L or C, or forgetting that capacitor current depends on dv/dt and inductor voltage on di/dt.
chapters.leave: Series and parallel element combinations, and time-domain transients, go to 1.5 and Unit 5.

chapters.idea: An independent source sets its own voltage or current; a dependent source sets its output as a fixed multiple of a voltage or current elsewhere.
chapters.depth: Ideal voltage source: fixed v, any i. Ideal current source: fixed i, any v. Practical source = ideal source plus internal resistance. Dependent sources: VCVS v = μ v_x (μ dimensionless), VCCS i = g v_x (g in siemens, S), CCVS v = r i_x (r in ohms), CCCS i = β i_x (β dimensionless). Use the diamond symbol.

figure.title: Four dependent sources
figure.aria: A control variable feeds four dependent-source boxes labelled VCVS, VCCS, CCVS and CCCS.

chapters.example: A VCVS has μ = 5 and v_x = 3 V, so output v = 15 V. A VCCS has g = 2 mS and v_x = 4 V, so output i = 8 mA. A CCVS has r = 10 Ω and i_x = 0.5 A, so output v = 5 V. A CCCS has β = 20 and i_x = 20 mA, so output i = 400 mA.
chapters.trap: Forgetting the unit of each gain: μ and β are pure numbers, g is in siemens, r is in ohms.
chapters.leave: Controlled-source equations inside mesh, nodal, Thevenin and Norton work go to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Ohm's law ties voltage and current in a resistor; KCL and KVL are conservation of charge and energy written at nodes and around loops.
chapters.depth: State Ohm's law v = iR, conductance G = 1/R in siemens. KCL: algebraic sum of currents at a node is zero, Σi = 0. KVL: algebraic sum of voltages around a closed loop is zero, Σv = 0. Fix a sign convention: choose entering currents positive or leaving positive, and stay with it. Cover open circuit (i = 0, v any) and short circuit (v = 0, i any). Apply to DC and AC; for AC the same laws hold for phasors (Unit 3).

figure.title: KCL and KVL
figure.aria: A flow from assigning signs to KCL and KVL, then to solving and checking equations.

chapters.example: At a node, 2 A enters. 0.8 A and 0.5 A leave through two resistors. Find the third leaving current I3: 2 = 0.8 + 0.5 + I3, so I3 = 0.7 A. Around a loop, a 12 V source has drops of 3 V and 5 V. Find Vx: 12 = 3 + 5 + Vx, so Vx = 4 V. A 12 Ω resistor carries 0.5 A, so its voltage is 6 V.
chapters.trap: Mixing entering and leaving currents, or adding voltage rises and drops with the same sign.
chapters.leave: Phasor form of KCL and KVL, and mesh/nodal solution methods, go to Unit 2 and Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A circuit has a small set of named parts, and counting them tells how many independent equations are needed.
chapters.depth: Node: a point where two or more elements meet; some syllabi call a node with three or more elements a junction. Branch: one element or a series path between nodes. Loop: any closed path. Mesh: a loop that contains no other loop; only planar circuits have meshes. Open circuit and short circuit as limiting branches. For a connected planar circuit, meshes = b − n + 1, node equations = n − 1. Define path and tree only as needed for 1.8.

figure.aria: A square graph with a diagonal branch; the square and the two triangles are loops, and the two triangles are meshes.

chapters.example: A connected planar circuit has n = 4 nodes and b = 6 branches. A tree has n − 1 = 3 branches. Chords = b − n + 1 = 3. Meshes = 3. Independent node equations = n − 1 = 3.
chapters.trap: Calling every node a junction, or counting a mesh in a non-planar drawing.
chapters.leave: Mesh and nodal analysis, supermesh and supernode, go to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Series and parallel rules collapse many resistors into one, and divider rules read one branch voltage or current without solving the whole circuit.
chapters.depth: Series: same current, R_eq = R1 + R2 + ...; parallel: same voltage, 1/R_eq = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ... For two resistors, R_eq = R1R2/(R1+R2). Voltage division: V_x = V_s R_x / R_total. Current division for two resistors: I1 = I_s R2/(R1+R2). Duality for L and C: series L adds, parallel C adds; parallel L and series C use reciprocals. Some syllabi call these network reduction techniques.

figure.title: Reduce to one resistor
figure.aria: Three boxes show series reduction, parallel reduction and divider rules in order.

chapters.example: A 12 V source feeds R1 = 6 Ω in series with a parallel pair R2 = 12 Ω and R3 = 6 Ω. Parallel value = 12×6/(12+6) = 4 Ω. Total = 6 + 4 = 10 Ω. Source current = 12/10 = 1.2 A. Voltage across the parallel pair = 1.2 × 4 = 4.8 V. Current in R2 = 4.8/12 = 0.4 A; current in R3 = 4.8/6 = 0.8 A.
chapters.trap: Using R1/(R1+R2) for the current through R2; the current divider ratio is reversed.
chapters.leave: Ladder and bridge circuits as full examples, and AC impedance dividers, go to Unit 2 and Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A three-terminal star of resistors can be replaced by a delta with the same terminal behaviour, and the reverse.
chapters.depth: Name nodes A, B, C and star centre N. Star resistors R_A, R_B, R_C; delta resistors R_AB, R_BC, R_CA. Delta to star: R_A = R_AB R_CA / (R_AB + R_BC + R_CA), and cyclic. Star to delta: R_AB = (R_A R_B + R_B R_C + R_C R_A)/R_C, and cyclic. Balanced case: R_Y = R_Δ/3, R_Δ = 3R_Y. Some syllabi call it Y-Δ or wye-delta. Use it to turn a bridge into series-parallel form.

figure.aria: A star of three resistors on the left and a delta of three resistors on the right, with matching labels.

chapters.example: A delta has R_AB = 10 Ω, R_BC = 20 Ω, R_CA = 30 Ω. Sum = 60 Ω. R_A = 10×30/60 = 5 Ω. R_B = 10×20/60 = 3.333 Ω. R_C = 20×30/60 = 10 Ω. The star replaces the delta at terminals A, B, C.
chapters.trap: Putting the numerator resistors in the wrong order; each star resistor is the product of the two delta resistors touching that node divided by the delta sum.
chapters.leave: Full bridge and ladder reduction practice, and AC bridge applications, go to Unit 2 and Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A practical voltage source and a practical current source are two models of the same terminal behaviour when V_s = I_s R_s.
chapters.depth: Voltage source V_s in series with R_s becomes current source I_s = V_s/R_s in parallel with the same R_s. Reverse: I_s in parallel with R_s becomes V_s = I_s R_s in series with R_s. Keep the source arrow direction: the current source arrow points from the negative terminal to the positive terminal inside the source, so the terminal current leaves the positive terminal. Ideal sources cannot be transformed: series R_s = 0 or parallel R_s = ∞. Some syllabi call it source conversion.

figure.title: Source transformation
figure.aria: A voltage source with series resistance and a current source with parallel resistance are linked by replace and reverse arrows, both driving the same load.

chapters.example: A 24 V source has 6 Ω in series and feeds a 3 Ω load. Original current = 24/(6+3) = 2.667 A; load voltage = 8 V. Transform to I_s = 24/6 = 4 A in parallel with 6 Ω. Load current = 4 × 6/(6+3) = 2.667 A; load voltage = 8 V.
chapters.trap: Reversing the current-source arrow, or transforming an ideal source with no series resistance.
chapters.leave: Dependent-source transformations and source transformation inside Thevenin/Norton proofs go to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: A circuit diagram can be read as a graph, and a tree picks a small set of tie-sets and cut-sets that give independent KVL and KCL equations.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Define graph, oriented graph, tree, co-tree, chord. For a connected graph with n nodes and b branches: tree has n−1 branches, co-tree has b−n+1 chords; fundamental tie-sets (loops) = b−n+1; fundamental cut-sets = n−1. A tie-set is one chord plus its unique tree path. A cut-set is a set of branches whose removal splits the graph; a fundamental cut-set has one tree branch. Show tie-set matrix rows and cut-set matrix rows. Keep to counting and one small graph.

figure.aria: A four-node graph with solid tree branches, dashed chords, and one chord closing a tie-set.

chapters.example: A connected graph has n = 5 nodes and b = 8 branches. Tree branches = n − 1 = 4. Chords = b − n + 1 = 4. Fundamental tie-sets = 4. Fundamental cut-sets = 4. One tie-set uses one chord plus its unique path through the tree.
chapters.trap: Using n instead of n−1 for tree branches, or b−n instead of b−n+1 for chords.
chapters.leave: Full mesh/nodal matrix methods and Tellegen's theorem go to Unit 2.
